extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory; policymakers and scholars interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the normative criteria Alexis de Tocqueville uses to diagnose dangers, mitigants, and social effects of the 'tyranny of the majority' in democratic republics (especially the United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority's combined physical and moral power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The authority of a king is purely physical, and it controls the actions of the subject without subduing his private will; but the majority possesses a power which is physical and moral at the same time; it acts upon the will as well as upon the actions of men, and it represses not only all contest, but all controversy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville contrasts monarchical physical coercion with democratic social/moral coercion: majority rule not only constrains actions but shapes private belief and silences debate. This criterion identifies when social majority translates into pervasive normative pressure beyond legal force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social ostracism as instrument of democratic despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors or individuals who stray beyond accepted opinion are not executed but are 'tormented by the slights and persecutions of daily obloquy' — deprived of political career, celebrity, and social support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate oppression in democracies by the presence of non-legal sanctions (shunning, loss of patronage, ridicule) that effectively coerce conformity and silence dissent, even where physical punishments are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of opinion as prerequisite for literary and intellectual genius
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘There can be no literary genius without freedom of opinion, and freedom of opinion does not exist in America.’ Because public opinion forbids certain publications and authors self-censor, great writers are less likely to appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the cultural effects of majoritarian pressure by measuring whether dissenting or unpopular ideas are publicly expressed and published; lack of public organs for heterodox thought indicates a constraint on cultural/intellectual creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic extension of currying favor degrades character
rubrics_metrics.description: Democratic republics 'extend the practice of currying favor with the many' and introduce servility into many classes, producing a 'far more extensive debasement of the characters of citizens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prevalence of behavior aimed at pleasing broad popular opinion (opportunism, performative loyalty) as an indicator of moral/political degradation produced by democratized access to power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public self-applause and intolerance of reproach
rubrics_metrics.description: The majority lives in 'the perpetual practice of self-applause,' where 'the smallest reproach irritates its sensibility' and even slight jokes provoke indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the capacity of the majority to accept criticism: communities that demand unqualified praise and react strongly against reproach demonstrate a social environment hostile to genuine critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of citizens to self-censor in public despite private dissent
rubrics_metrics.description: Many privately dissenting Americans 'continue to hold a different language in public' and only confide 'secret reflections' to foreigners; public condemnation and silent abandonment follow public dissent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the gap between private beliefs and public speech; a large discrepancy suggests social mechanisms (shame, career cost) that suppress public expression of minority views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatest danger: misuse of unlimited majority authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If free institutions are destroyed it may be 'attributed to the unlimited authority of the majority,' which can drive minorities to desperation and provoke physical force and anarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional risk by the scope of majoritarian power: when the majority's authority is unchecked and absolute, the potential for oppression and subsequent violent breakdown grows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between centralized government and centralized administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A central government may exist without a centralized administration; in the United States the majority is powerful but 'the latter [centralized administration] is nearly unknown' — central decrees must be executed by local agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the administrative reach of central authority: limited administrative penetration into local detail is a mitigating factor against majoritarian tyranny because execution depends on independent local officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local bodies (townships/counties) as administrative ‘break‑waters’
rubrics_metrics.description: Townships, municipal bodies, and counties act as 'concealed break-waters' that check the tide of popular excitement; even oppressive laws are mitigated by the means of their execution at local levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resilience to central overreach by the strength and autonomy of local governments; decentralized execution channels reduce the majority's ability to enforce uniform administrative tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal profession as aristocratic counterpoise to democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the legal profession possess 'habits of order, a taste for formalities, and a kind of instinctive regard for the regular connection of ideas,' which give them a conservative, aristocratic turn and make them a counterbalance to democratic excesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the role of lawyers and judges as institutional actors who, through training and occupation, can check populist impulses and stabilize government—especially where they occupy high public office or judiciary positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent-based law fosters conservatism and deference to the past
rubrics_metrics.description: English and American lawyers 'continue to found their legal opinions...upon the opinions and the decisions of their forefathers' — this 'reverence for what is old' produces timid habits and reluctance to innovate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the prevalence of common-law/precedent reasoning versus doctrinal reform as a gauge of legal conservatism; a strong precedent culture tends to slow rapid democratic reforms and protect stability (but may stifle needed change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial power as visible organ to control democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge, 'armed with the power of declaring the laws to be unconstitutional,' 'perpetually interferes in political affairs' and can oblige the people not to disobey its own enactments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the independence and scope of the judiciary: effective judicial review and independence from legislative removal/election increase the judiciary's capacity to check majoritarian abuses; conversely, easy removal or politicization weakens this safeguard.
